{{Short description|Software to detect AI-generated content}}
{{Artificial intelligence}}
{{Update|date=July 2026}}
'''Artificial intelligence detection software''' aims to determine whether some [[Content creation|content]] (text, image, video, or audio) was [[Generative AI|generated]] using [[artificial intelligence]] (AI). This software is often unreliable.<ref name="Fortune">{{Cite web |title='Don't use AI detectors for anything important,' says the author of the definitive 'AI Weirdness' blog. Her own book failed the test |url=https://fortune.com/2023/07/03/janelle-shane-ai-weirdness-dont-use-detectors-for-anything-important/ |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=Fortune |language=en}}</ref>

== Accuracy issues ==
Many AI detection tools have been shown to be unreliable in detecting AI-generated text. In a 2023 study conducted by Weber-Wulff et al., researchers evaluated 14 detection tools including [[Turnitin]] and [[GPTZero]] and found that "all scored below 80% of accuracy and only 5 over 70%."<ref name="WeberWulff-2023">{{Cite journal |last1=Weber-Wulff |first1=Debora |last2=Anohina-Naumeca |first2=Alla |last3=Bjelobaba |first3=Sonja |last4=Foltýnek |first4=Tomáš |last5=Guerrero-Dib |first5=Jean |last6=Popoola |first6=Olumide |last7=Šigut |first7=Petr |last8=Waddington |first8=Lorna |date=2023-12-25 |title=Testing of detection tools for AI-generated text |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-023-00146-z |journal=International Journal for Educational Integrity |language=en |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=26 |doi=10.1007/s40979-023-00146-z |issn=1833-2595|arxiv=2306.15666 }}</ref> They also found that these tools tend to have a bias for classifying texts more as human than as AI, and that accuracy of these tools worsens upon paraphrasing.<ref name="WeberWulff-2023" />

=== False positives ===
In AI content detection, a [[False positives and false negatives|false positive]] is when human-written work is incorrectly flagged as AI-written. Many AI detection platforms claim to have a minimal level of false positives, with Turnitin claiming a less than 1% false positive rate.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-03-16 |title=Understanding false positives within our AI writing detection capabilities |url=https://www.turnitin.com/blog/understanding-false-positives-within-our-ai-writing-detection-capabilities |access-date=2025-03-19 |website=www.turnitin.com |language=en-us}}</ref> However, later research by [[The Washington Post]] produced much higher rates of 50%, though they used a smaller sample size.<ref name="Fowler-2023a">{{Cite news |last1=Fowler |first1=Geoffrey A. |last2=Ovide |first2=Shira |date=2023-04-01 |title=We tested a new ChatGPT detector for teachers. It flagged an innocent student. |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2023/04/01/chatgpt-cheating-detection-turnitin/ |access-date=2025-03-19 |newspaper=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> False positives in an academic setting frequently lead to accusations of [[Academic dishonesty|academic misconduct]], which can have serious consequences for a student's [[Transcript (education)|academic record]]. Additionally, studies have shown evidence that many AI detection models are prone to give false positives to work written by people whose [[first language]] is not [[English language|English]],  and also to [[neurodivergence|neurodivergent]] people.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AI-Detectors Biased Against Non-Native English Writers {{!}} Stanford HAI |url=https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-detectors-biased-against-non-native-english-writers |access-date=2025-03-20 |website=hai.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Challenge of AI Checkers {{!}} Center for Transformative Teaching {{!}} Nebraska |url=https://teaching.unl.edu/ai-exchange/challenge-ai-checkers/ |access-date=2025-03-20 |website=teaching.unl.edu |language=en}}</ref>

In June 2023, [[Janelle Shane]] wrote that portions of her book ''[[You Look Like a Thing and I Love You]]'' were flagged as AI-generated.<ref name="Fortune" />

=== False negatives ===
A [[False positives and false negatives|false negative]] is a failure to identify documents with AI-written text. False negatives often happen as a result of a detection software's [[Sensitivity and specificity|sensitivity]] level or because evasive techniques were used when generating the work to make it sound more human.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Condit |first=Cynthia |title=LibGuides: ChatGPT and Generative AI Legal Research Guide: AI Detection Tools |url=https://law-arizona.libguides.com/c.php?g=1301273&p=9750512 |access-date=2025-03-20 |website=law-arizona.libguides.com |language=en}}</ref> False negatives are less of a concern academically, since they aren't likely to lead to accusations and ramifications. Notably, Turnitin stated they have a 15% false negative rate.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Turnitin adding AI writing detection, but instructors should use it with caution |url=https://www.purdue.edu/online/turnitin-adding-ai-writing-detection-but-instructors-should-use-it-with-caution/ |access-date=2025-03-20 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Text detection ==
For text, this is usually done to prevent alleged [[plagiarism]], often by detecting repetition of words as telltale signs that a text was AI-generated (including [[Hallucination (artificial intelligence)|hallucinations]]).  Detection systems may also rely on stylistic and structural regularities associated with LLM output, such as unusually consistent grammar, formulaic transitions, repeated discourse markers, and recurring rhetorical templates. Some tools are designed less to establish authorship provenance than to flag prose that resembles common LLM-generated style patterns.

AI text detectors may analyze textual predictability, repeated wording, and variation in sentence structure, but their outputs are probabilistic assessments rather than definitive proof of authorship.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.zerogpt.plus/blog/ai-detection-explained-how-it-works-what-to-watch-for-and-using-ai-the-right-way/|title=AI Detection Explained: How It Works, What to Watch For, and Using AI the Right Way|author=Content Team|website=ZeroGPT Plus Blog|publisher=ZeroGPT Plus|access-date=July 27, 2026|language=en}}</ref>

They are often used by teachers marking their students, usually on an ''[[ad hoc]]'' basis. Following the release of [[ChatGPT]] and similar AI text generative software, many educational establishments have issued policies against the use of AI by students.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hern |first1=Alex |title=AI-assisted plagiarism? ChatGPT bot says it has an answer for that |url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2022/dec/31/ai-assisted-plagiarism-chatgpt-bot-says-it-has-an-answer-for-that |access-date=11 July 2023 |work=The Guardian |date=31 December 2022}}</ref> AI text detection software is also used by those assessing job applicants, as well as online [[search engines]],<ref name="Sample">{{cite news |last1=Sample |first1=Ian |title=Programs to detect AI discriminate against non-native English speakers, shows study |url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2023/jul/10/programs-to-detect-ai-discriminate-against-non-native-english-speakers-shows-study |access-date=10 July 2023 |work=The Guardian |date=10 July 2023}}</ref> hiring, online moderation and publishing.

Current detectors may sometimes be unreliable and have incorrectly marked work by humans as originating from AI<ref name="Fowler-2023b">{{cite news |last1=Fowler |first1=Geoffrey A. |title=Detecting AI may be impossible. That's a big problem for teachers. |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2023/06/02/turnitin-ai-cheating-detector-accuracy/ |access-date=10 July 2023 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=2 June 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Tangermann |first1=Victor |title=There's a Problem With That App That Detects GPT-Written Text: It's Not Very Accurate |url=https://futurism.com/gptzero-accuracy |access-date=10 July 2023 |work=Futurism |date=9 January 2023}}</ref><ref name="Fowler-2023a" /> while failing to detect AI-generated work in other instances.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Taylor |first1=Josh |title=ChatGPT maker OpenAI releases 'not fully reliable' tool to detect AI generated content |url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2023/feb/01/chatgpt-maker-openai-releases-ai-generated-content-detection-tool |access-date=11 July 2023 |work=The Guardian |date=1 February 2023}}</ref> ''[[MIT Technology Review]]'' said that the technology "struggled to pick up ChatGPT-generated text that had been slightly rearranged by humans and obfuscated by a paraphrasing tool".<ref name="Williams">{{cite news |last1=Williams |first1=Rhiannon |title=AI-text detection tools are really easy to fool|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2023/07/07/1075982/ai-text-detection-tools-are-really-easy-to-fool/ |access-date=10 July 2023 |work=MIT Technology Review |date=7 July 2023}}</ref> AI text detection software has also been shown to discriminate against non-native speakers of English.<ref name="Sample"/>

Two students from the [[University of California, Davis]], were referred to the university's Office of Student Success and Judicial Affairs (OSSJA) after their professors scanned their essays with positive results; the first with an AI detector called GPTZero, and the second with an AI detector integration in [[Turnitin]]. However, following media coverage,<ref>{{Cite web |title=AI Detection Apps Keep Falsely Accusing Students of Cheating |url=https://futurism.com/ai-plagiarism-software-false-accusing-students |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=Futurism|date=6 June 2023 }}</ref> and a thorough investigation, the students were cleared of any wrongdoing.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jimenez |first=Kayla |title=Professors are using ChatGPT detector tools to accuse students of cheating. But what if the software is wrong? |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/education/2023/04/12/how-ai-detection-tool-spawned-false-cheating-case-uc-davis/11600777002/ |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Klee |first=Miles |date=2023-06-06 |title=She Was Falsely Accused of Cheating With AI -- And She Won't Be the Last |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/culture/culture-features/student-accused-ai-cheating-turnitin-1234747351/ |access-date=2023-10-21 |magazine=Rolling Stone |language=en-US}}</ref>

In April 2023, [[Cambridge University]] and other members of the [[Russell Group]] of universities in the United Kingdom opted out of Turnitin's AI text detection tool, after expressing concerns it was unreliable.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Staton |first1=Bethan |date=3 April 2023 |title=Universities express doubt over tool to detect AI-powered plagiarism |work=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/d872d65d-dfd0-40b3-8db9-a17fea20c60c |access-date=10 July 2023}}</ref> The [[University of Texas at Austin]] opted out of the system six months later.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Carter |first=Tom |title=Some universities are ditching AI detection software amid fears students could be falsely accused of cheating by using ChatGPT |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/universities-ditch-ai-detectors-over-fears-students-falsely-accused-cheating-2023-9 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=Business Insider |language=en-US}}</ref>

In May 2023, a professor at [[East Texas A&M University|Texas A&M University–Commerce]] used ChatGPT to detect whether his students' content was written by it, which ChatGPT said was the case. As such, he threatened to fail the class despite ChatGPT not being able to detect AI-generated writing.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Verma |first1=Prashnu |title=A professor accused his class of using ChatGPT, putting diplomas in jeopardy |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2023/05/18/texas-professor-threatened-fail-class-chatgpt-cheating/ |access-date=10 July 2023 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=18 May 2023}}</ref> No students were prevented from graduating because of the issue, and all but one student (who admitted to using the software) were exonerated from accusations of having used ChatGPT in their content.<ref>{{cite news |title=College instructor put on blast for accusing students of using ChatGPT |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/chatgpt-texas-college-instructor-backlash-rcna84888 |access-date=10 July 2023 |work=NBC News |date=18 May 2023}}</ref>

In July 2023, a paper titled "GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers" was released, reporting that GPTs discriminate against non-native English authors. The paper compared seven GPT detectors against essays from both non-native English speakers and essays from United States students. The essays from non-native English speakers had an average false positive rate of 61.3%.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Liang |first1=Weixin |last2=Yuksekgonul |first2=Mert |last3=Mao |first3=Yining |last4=Wu |first4=Eric |last5=Zou |first5=James |date=14 July 2023 |title=GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers |volume=4 |issue=7 |doi=10.1016/j.patter.2023.100779 |doi-access=free |journal=Patterns |article-number=100779 |pmid=37521038 |pmc=10382961 }}</ref>

An article by Thomas Germain, published on [[Gizmodo]] in June 2024, reported job losses among freelance writers and journalists due to AI text detection software mistakenly classifying their work as AI-generated.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Germain |first=Thomas |date=2024-06-12 |title=AI Detectors Get It Wrong. Writers Are Being Fired Anyway |url=https://gizmodo.com/ai-detectors-inaccurate-freelance-writers-fired-1851529820 |access-date=2024-06-18 |website=Gizmodo |language=en}}</ref>

In September 2024, [[Common Sense Media]] reported that generative AI detectors had a 20% false positive rate for Black students, compared to 10% of Latino students and 7% of White students.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Madden |first1=Mary |last2=Calvin |first2=Angela |last3=Hasse |first3=Alexa |last4=Lenhart |first4=Amanda |date=18 September 2024 |title=The Dawn of the AI Era |page=10<!-- 10 is the page number displayed on the PDF page; 15 is the page number offset in the PDF --> |url=https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/research/report/2024-the-dawn-of-the-ai-era_final-release-for-web.pdf#page=15 |website=[[Common Sense Media]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250424233647/https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/research/report/2024-the-dawn-of-the-ai-era_final-release-for-web.pdf#page=15 |archive-date=24 April 2025 |access-date=26 May 2025 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Klein |first= Alyson |date=18 September 2024 |title=Black Students Are More Likely to Be Falsely Accused of Using AI to Cheat |url=https://www.edweek.org/technology/black-students-are-more-likely-to-be-falsely-accused-of-using-ai-to-cheat/2024/09 |website=[[Education Week]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250502010046/https://www.edweek.org/technology/black-students-are-more-likely-to-be-falsely-accused-of-using-ai-to-cheat/2024/09 |archive-date=2 May 2025 |access-date=26 May 2025}}</ref>

To improve the reliability of AI text detection, researchers have explored [[digital watermarking]] techniques (see [[Text watermarking]]). A 2023 paper titled "A Watermark for Large Language Models"<ref name="Kirchenbauer-2023">{{Cite journal |arxiv=2301.10226 |last1=Kirchenbauer |first1=Johannes |last2=Geiping |first2=Jonas |last3=Wen |first3=Yuxin |last4=Katz |first4=Jonathan |last5=Miers |first5=Ian |last6=Goldstein |first6=Tom |date=2023-06-24 |title=Testing of detection tools for AI-generated text |journal=International Journal for Educational Integrity |volume=19 |article-number=26 |doi=10.1007/s40979-023-00146-z |language=en }}</ref> presents a method to embed imperceptible watermarks into text generated by [[large language models]] (LLMs). This watermarking approach allows content to be flagged as AI-generated with a high level of accuracy, even when text is slightly paraphrased or modified. The technique is designed to be subtle and hard to detect for casual readers, thereby preserving readability, while providing a detectable signal for those employing specialized tools. However, while promising, watermarking faces challenges in remaining robust under adversarial transformations and ensuring compatibility across different LLMs.

== Anti text detection ==
There is software available designed to bypass AI text detection.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Beam |first=Christopher |title=The AI Detection Arms Race Is On—and College Students Are Building the Weapons |language=en-US |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/story/ai-detection-chat-gpt-college-students/ |access-date=2023-12-02 |issn=1059-1028}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Lee |first=Maxie |date=August 8, 2025 |title=Is Undetectable AI Legit? 2025 Review, Accuracy & User Insights |url=https://humanizerai.com/blog/is-undetectable-ai-legit-2025 |work=Humanizer Ai }}</ref>

In practice, evasion may not require specialized bypass tools. Paraphrasing, style editing, and removal of repeated discourse markers can substantially reduce the effectiveness of detectors that rely on recognizable surface patterns. A study published in August 2023 analyzed 20 abstracts from papers published in the [[Eye (journal)|Eye Journal]], which were then paraphrased using [[GPT-4]].0. The AI-paraphrased abstracts were examined for plagiarism using QueText and for AI-generated content using Originality.AI. The texts were then re-processed through an [[Adversarial machine learning|adversarial software]] called [[Undetectable.ai]] in order to reduce the AI-detection scores. The study found that the AI detection tool, Originality.AI, identified text generated by GPT-4 with a mean accuracy of 91.3%. However, after reprocessing by Undetectable.ai, the detection accuracy of Originality.ai dropped to a mean accuracy of 27.8%.<ref name="Taloni-2023">{{Cite journal |last1=Taloni |first1=Andrea |last2=Scorcia |first2=Vincenzo |last3=Giannaccare |first3=Giuseppe |date=2023-08-02 |title=Modern threats in academia: evaluating plagiarism and artificial intelligence detection scores of ChatGPT |journal=Eye |language=en |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=397–400 |doi=10.1038/s41433-023-02678-7 |issn=1476-5454 |pmid=37532832 |pmc=10810838 }}</ref>

Some experts also believe that techniques like [[digital watermarking]] are ineffective because they can be removed or added to trigger false positives.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Knibbs |first=Kate |title=Researchers Tested AI Watermarks—and Broke All of Them |language=en-US |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/story/artificial-intelligence-watermarking-issues/ |access-date=2023-10-21 |issn=1059-1028}}</ref> "A Watermark for Large Language Models" paper by Kirchenbauer et al. (2023) <ref name="Kirchenbauer-2023"/> also addresses potential vulnerabilities of watermarking techniques. The authors outline a range of adversarial tactics, including text insertion, deletion, and substitution attacks, that could be used to bypass watermark detection. These attacks vary in complexity, from simple paraphrasing to more sophisticated approaches involving [[Tokenization (lexical analysis)|tokenization]] and homoglyph alterations. The study highlights the challenge of maintaining watermark robustness against attackers who may employ automated [[paraphrasing]] tools or even specific language model replacements to alter text spans iteratively while retaining semantic similarity. Experimental results show that although such attacks can degrade watermark strength, they also come at the cost of text quality and increased computational resources. 

== Image, video, and audio detection ==
Several purported AI image detection software exist, to detect AI-generated images (for example, those originating from [[Midjourney]] or [[DALL-E]]). They are not completely reliable.<ref name="ThoHsu">{{cite news |last1=Thompson |first1=Stuart A. |last2=Hsu |first2=Tiffany |title=How Easy Is It to Fool A.I.-Detection Tools? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/06/28/technology/ai-detection-midjourney-stable-diffusion-dalle.html |access-date=10 July 2023 |work=The New York Times |date=28 June 2023}}</ref><ref name="Rizwan-2023">{{Cite news |last=Rizwan |first=Choudhury |date=October 15, 2023 |title=Expert debunks AI tool's claim that Israel's photo is fake |work=Interesting Engineering |url=https://interestingengineering.com/culture/expert-debunks-ai-tools-claim-that-israels-photo-is-fake |access-date=October 22, 2023}}</ref>

Industry analyses have also noted that AI-driven image recognition systems often struggle in real-world environments, where inconsistent lighting, noise and variable visual inputs reduce detection reliability, a challenge highlighted in modern agricultural quality-control research.<ref name="ForbesAgriAI">{{cite news |last=Hamal |first=Ihor |title=Digital Quality Control: The New Edge In Agriculture |work=Forbes |date=24 September 2025 |url=https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbesbusinesscouncil/2025/09/24/digital-quality-control-the-new-edge-in-agriculture/ |access-date=4 December 2025}}</ref>

Others claim to identify video and audio [[deepfake]]s, but this technology is also not fully reliable yet either.<ref name="MyeHsu">{{cite news |last1=Hsu |first1=Tiffany |last2=Myers |first2=Steven Lee |title=Another Side of the A.I. Boom: Detecting What A.I. Makes |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/18/technology/ai-chat-gpt-detection-tools.html |access-date=10 July 2023 |work=The New York Times |date=18 May 2023}}</ref>

Despite debate around the efficacy of watermarking, [[Google DeepMind]] is actively developing a detection software called SynthID, which works by inserting a digital watermark that is invisible to the human eye into the [[pixel]]s of an image.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pierce |first=David |date=2023-08-29 |title=Google made a watermark for AI images that you can't edit out |url=https://www.theverge.com/2023/8/29/23849107/synthid-google-deepmind-ai-image-detector |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Verge}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wiggers |first=Kyle |date=2023-08-29 |title=DeepMind partners with Google Cloud to watermark AI-generated images |url=https://techcrunch.com/2023/08/29/deepmind-partners-with-google-cloud-to-watermark-ai-generated-images/ |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=TechCrunch}}</ref>
